AQL GUIDE · FOUNDATIONS

Categories & Tags

The Taxonomy filters item in the AQL: Taxonomy panel filters by how content is organized — categories, tags, or any custom grouping — and lets you combine rules. Each card below shows its categories and tags so you can check the filter's work.

Posts in a category

One rule: the post is in the Engineering category. Because "include children" is on, posts in Engineering's sub-categories (like WordPress and JavaScript) count too.

Nothing matched.

In one group, but not another

Two rules combined with AND: in the Engineering category, but not tagged "experimental". Compare with the list above — the experimental posts have dropped out.

Nothing matched.

Try these changes

  1. Turn off "include children" on the first query — posts filed only under WordPress or JavaScript disappear.
  2. Swap the first query's category from Engineering to Design.
  3. Turn on Advanced mode for a rule to reach the full set of operators.

AQL GUIDE · FOUNDATIONS

Custom Fields

Custom fields are extra facts attached to a post — a rating, a price, a yes/no flag. The Meta filters item in the AQL: Meta panel turns them into filters. The recipes here carry two fields: a rating and a featured flag.

One filter: only the editor's picks

A single condition: the featured field equals "yes". Three recipes qualify.

No recipes matched.

Two filters with AND: featured and highly rated

Add a second condition and choose AND: a recipe must be featured and rated 4 or better. The list tightens.

No recipes matched.

Two filters with OR: either one counts

Switch the relationship to OR and a recipe only needs to pass one test: featured, or rated 2 and under (say, a "loved or overlooked" list). The list widens.

No recipes matched.

Try these changes

  1. Change the rating threshold from 4 to 5 in the AND query.
  2. Flip the AND query to OR and compare the two lists.
  3. Pair this with the Order By guide: sort the featured list by rating, highest first.

AQL GUIDE · FOUNDATIONS

Dates

The AQL: Date panel filters by publish date two ways: a Dynamic range that keeps itself up to date ("the last three months"), or a Date relationship pinned to a specific date ("everything before January 2025").

Dynamic range: recent posts, automatically

This list shows posts from the last three months — and it will still say that next year, with no edits, because the range moves with today's date. Check the dates on the cards.

Nothing published in the last three months.

Date relationship: before a specific date

A fixed cutoff works the other way — it never moves. This list only shows posts published before January 1, 2025, which on this site means the recipe archive.

Nothing published before that date.

Try these changes

  1. Switch the dynamic range to Last month and watch the list shrink.
  2. Change the relationship from Before to After — the two lists trade places.
  3. Try Between with two dates to build a "from the archives" list for one specific stretch.

AQL RECIPE · FOUNDATIONS

Order By

The AQL: Order by panel controls the order posts appear in. Start with a single property, sort by a custom field, or add a secondary sort to settle ties. Every example below queries the same recipe posts so the differences are easy to spot.

Pick the order

The Order item holds two settings: the property to sort by and the direction. This query orders posts by title, A to Z.

No recipes matched.

Sort by a custom field

Choose Meta Value (Numeric) as the property and a Meta key to sort by field appears. This query sorts by a numeric rating field, highest first — and recipes without a rating stay in the list, at the end.

No recipes matched.

Using a secondary sort

When two posts match on the main property, a secondary sort decides who goes first. Add Secondary sort from the panel menu and pick its own property and direction. This query orders by publish date, and recipes published the same day line up alphabetically instead of at random.

No recipes matched.

Both together: featured first, newest on top

The two ideas combine naturally. Here the main sort is a featured custom field, so editor's picks rise to the top, and the secondary sort keeps each group in date order.

AQL GUIDE · UNDER THE HOOD

Performance

The AQL: Performance panel is the only one whose results you shouldn't see. Both switches make the page do less work behind the scenes — the lists look identical, they're just cheaper.

Pagination: skip the counting

To draw page numbers, WordPress has to count every matching post — even the ones it isn't showing. A "top 4" list like this one will never have page links, so the Pagination switch is off and that counting is skipped entirely.

Caching: remember the answer

With Caching on, the site saves this query's results and reuses them for later visitors instead of asking the database again. It looks exactly like any other list — that's the point. Use it for queries that don't change often, like this year-in-review of the lowest-rated experiments.

No recipes matched.

Good to know

  • Leave Pagination on whenever the list actually shows page links — turning it off breaks them.
  • Cached results refresh on a timer, so a brand-new post may take a little while to appear in a cached list.
  • These switches matter most on big sites with thousands of posts; on a small site you won't feel the difference — and that's fine.

AQL GUIDE · FOUNDATIONS

Post Types & Picking Posts

The AQL: Post panel decides what is in your list: which content types, which exact posts, which posts to leave out, and whether to show only child items.

Post types: mix content in one list

Normally a Query Loop shows one content type. Add more under Post types and they all appear together — here Posts, Projects, and Guides share one alphabetical list, each card labeled with its type.

Exclude current post: no déjà vu

On a "related content" list you never want the page the visitor is already reading. The guide list below has Exclude current post switched on — notice this very guide is missing from it.

Child items only: just the sub-pages

For content organized under a parent — chapters under a handbook, sub-pages under a page — Child items only narrows the list to one family. This query shows only the guides filed under Start Here — including the one you're reading.

AQL RECIPE · FOUNDATIONS

Build a mixed-content query

Start with a normal Query block, choose the Advanced Query Loop variation, then layer AQL controls onto the core query settings.

Posts and Projects together

AQL GUIDE · UNDER THE HOOD

Query ID

The Query ID field in the AQL: Advanced panel gives a query a name. It changes nothing on its own — it's a label a developer can use to find this exact query in code and customize it beyond what the panels offer.

Name the query

The list below is named recipes-spotlight. Select it in the editor, open AQL: Advanced, and you'll see the name in the Query ID field. Pick names the way you'd name a file — short, descriptive, no spaces.

No recipes matched.

Hand the name to your developer

That name is the whole hand-off. A developer can now target just this query — for example, to cap it at three results no matter what the block says:

add_filter( 'aql_query_vars', function ( $query_args, $block_query, $inherited ) {
	if ( 'recipes-spotlight' === ( $block_query['aql_query_id'] ?? '' ) ) {
		$query_args['posts_per_page'] = 3;
	}
	return $query_args;
}, 10, 3 );

Every other query on the site is untouched — that's what the name buys you.

Good to know

  • Names don't need to be unique, but giving two queries the same name means code targeting it affects both.
  • Renaming a query breaks any code targeting the old name — treat a name as a promise.
  • Every example query in these guides carries an ID — select any of them and peek at AQL: Advanced.

AQL GUIDE · GETTING STARTED

Start Here

Advanced Query Loop is the normal Query Loop block with extra settings. If you can add a Query Loop, you can use everything in these guides — no code required.

Add the block

In the editor, add a block and search for Advanced Query Loop. Already have a Query Loop on the page? Select it, open its block menu, and transform it into Advanced Query Loop — your existing settings come along.

Where the settings live

With the block selected, the sidebar gains a set of panels, each starting with AQL:. Each one has its own guide:

  • AQL: Post — mix content types, hand-pick or leave out posts, show child items.
  • AQL: Order by — control the order, including ties.
  • AQL: Date — recent posts automatically, or before/after a date.
  • AQL: Meta — filter by custom fields.
  • AQL: Taxonomy — filter by categories, tags, and more.
  • AQL: Performance — pagination and caching.
  • AQL: Advanced — name a query for a developer.
